source.title: Standard SAEs Might Be Incoherent: A Choosing Problem & A “Concise” Solution

page_placements.theme: SAE objectives admit low-loss solutions that differ from the true features (theory and toy)

record.tranche_reason: The post argues that standard SAEs can yield non-unique explanatory mediators and illustrates this with a same-dictionary example. It does not test whether increasing dictionary size splits features, whether split features partition inputs, or any of the other version-specific behaviors.
record.gate_note: The post discusses feature splitting as a separate problem motivating MDL-SAEs, but reports no size sweep or test of splitting. Its own theoretical construction and Gemma Scope example concern alternative encodings of the same activation within one dictionary; these are recorded as findings under none of the listed versions. Claims and results linked to other posts are not recorded as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The post argues that minimal sparse codes under one fixed standard-SAE dictionary are non-unique, and illustrates this with one approximate Gemma Scope 16K example. It mentions feature splitting only in passing, as a problem MDL-SAEs were proposed to address. It reports no dictionary-size sweep, no parent/child firing analysis, and no comparison across SAE sizes or objectives, so none of V1–V6 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct as paraphrased. The authors argue that the explain function defined by standard SAEs is ill-defined for any imperfect AutoInterp. They propose MDL-SAEs as a more principled formulation that generally gives a unique code, while noting it may not be the only solution.
record.recipe_differences: The post presents a theoretical argument and an illustrative SAE example; it does not reproduce or apply a feature-splitting measurement recipe.

fits_no_version.finding: Under one overcomplete dictionary, distinct k-sparse codes can decode to the same activation with equal L0. In Gemma Scope 16K layer 16, features 2861, 12998 and 16146 approximately satisfy f3≈f2−αf1, giving two approximately minimal codes with differing Neuronpedia explanations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Standard SAE explanations are non-unique: equally sparse, equally accurate codes for the same activation can yield different semantic explanations.

record.problems: The real-SAE illustration is approximate and is described as coming from a brief, unoptimised search; the post does not provide a systematic empirical evaluation. Its central argument is theoretical.

untested.parts: All: no comparison across dictionary sizes.
All: no splitting test in large models or open releases. The Gemma Scope example concerns non-uniqueness within one dictionary.
All: no feature families or hierarchy analysis.
All: no absorption or parent/child firing test.
All: no larger-versus-smaller SAE decomposition analysis.
All: MDL-SAEs are proposed as a remedy for splitting, but the post gives no result on whether splitting changes.

record.verdict_notes: r2's size field should read 'Gemma 2 2B, 16K-latent SAE', per the Neuronpedia URLs. The post's mention of feature splitting refers to the separate MDL-SAE post and is not a result here.

versions.untested_parts: No increasing-dictionary-size comparison or test of whether finer features cover a coarse feature's inputs and lie near its direction.
No splitting test in large models or across open SAE releases.
No test of nested feature families or whether they mirror a hierarchy of concepts.
No test of parent-child firing, absorption, or the effects of changing SAE size or sparsity on absorption.
No comparison of larger and smaller SAEs, nor a test for novel latents across dictionary sizes.
No test of whether splitting is caused by the SAE objective on correlated or hierarchical inputs, or whether Matryoshka SAEs change or reduce splitting.

rows.subject: constructed feature dictionary (not a model)
rows.operation_detail: Constructed two sparse feature-activation representations that decode to the same activation.

conditions.value: f1, f2, f3 = f1, f2, f2 − αf1, for α > −1

rows.measure: Whether distinct explanatory mediators can have the same decoded activation and L0 sparsity.
rows.value: z=(1,1,0,0,...) and z′=(α+1,0,1,0,...) decode to the same x; both have L0=2.
rows.locator: Section 2, example of feature directions and explanatory mediators
rows.note: A constructed example of non-uniqueness within one overcomplete dictionary, not a comparison across dictionary sizes.

rows.subject: Gemma 2
rows.operation_detail: Examined three Gemma Scope feature directions and compared two approximately equivalent sparse encodings and their Neuronpedia AutoInterp explanations.
rows.measure: Approximate relation between feature directions, equivalence of the resulting mediators, and consistency of their AutoInterp explanations.
rows.value: The text says f3≈f2−αf1; z and z′ are approximately minimal mediators for the same x. The AutoInterp explanations for z and z′ differ: one is described in terms of symbols and the other in terms of expressing inability in language.
rows.locator: Section 2, “Incoherency in the Wild with Gemma Scope”
rows.note: The post describes this as an approximate example found by an unoptimised search lasting a couple of minutes on a consumer laptop. It does not compare different SAE sizes or test feature splitting.

source_check.notes: This record is about non-unique sparse codes within one fixed dictionary, not splitting across dictionary sizes. The Gemma example is approximate and came from a few minutes of unoptimised search. Footnote 9 only speculates, without testing, that incoherence is worse for larger SAEs and larger k.

statements.problem: none. Text gives features 2861, 12998, 16146 as f1, f2, f3 in the Gemma Scope 16K layer-16 SAE, with f3≈f2−αf1 for α=1e-2. It says z and z′ are approximately minimal mediators for the same x. Their explanations differ: symbols versus expressing inability.
